reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents Terra Luna Classic supply-and-market-cap calculations and commentary about a possible future price, including claims attributed to a livestream guest. Although the title uses promotional language such as "Proof" and the speaker says the situation is "about to get insane," the supplied content does not show an explicit request to buy tokens, a guaranteed return, or a deceptive participation flow.

opening.argument: The video links a highly specific appreciation promise to the obvious viewer action of acquiring or holding the token, even without saying “buy” outright. Its title presents “Proof” that Terra Luna Classic can reach “$100 Per Coin,” while the narration supplies a mechanism for that outcome: supply could fall to “100 million coins,” and a billion-dollar market cap is presented alongside progressively higher prices. That framing turns market commentary into an implied participation pitch: viewers are invited to treat possession of the token as the way to benefit from the advertised upside. The closing language, “This shits about to get insane,” reinforces urgency and excitement rather than balanced financial analysis.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the content calculations does not answer its promotional structure. The title does not merely report a price; it calls the outcome “Proof” and names a dramatic target. The narration then highlights a path from reduced supply to much higher prices and ends with excitement. That combination can steer viewers toward acquiring or holding the asset even if the speaker omits a literal purchase instruction. Absence of an explicit deposit request does not make an implied appreciation pitch neutral.
